solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Hold it's ecstasy snuggling up to minute underwear around the end of June

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last of that month's letters is kept

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
M is the abbreviation for minute
a bra is an item of underwear
C, short for circa, means around
the last letter of June

explanation.surface: A seedy tableau of someone high on ecstasy, cuddling up to skimpy lingerie in late June.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold' looks like the start of an instruction ('hold it'), but it is the definition and 'it's' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To embrace someone is to hug them, a synonym of holding them in your arms.

clue.text: Quickly producing a book, say, The Wanker's Art

blocks.note: first meaning: dashing off a piece of writing with little effort
second meaning: British slang for masturbating

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's crossword is deliberately rude: the phrasal verb means both writing something hastily and, in British slang, masturbation.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for producing work quickly and also vulgar slang for self-pleasure, which a wanker practises.

clue.text: Grauniad's chief, well into yarn, is a bit of a pain

indicators.note: the chief letter of a word is its first, the one at its head
something placed well into something else sits deep inside it

blocks.note: first part of twine, a kind of yarn
first letter of Grauniad, Private Eye's nickname for the Guardian
the last letter of twine, closing around the inserted letter

explanation.surface: The Guardian's editor is deep in some story that proves mildly painful.
explanation.walkthrough: Twine (yarn) takes G near its end. The Grauniad is Private Eye's long-running nickname for the typo-prone Guardian newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinge is a sudden brief pang, a small amount of pain.

clue.text: Ms Short almost is, like, making a comeback – that's novel!

definitions.note: the answer is the title of a novel

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the surname is dropped
coming back means travelling the other way, so the word is read from end to start

blocks.note: Clare Short, the Labour MP
taken as written
as means like

explanation.surface: Clare Short is staging a political comeback, which would be a novelty.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare Short was a Labour cabinet minister; 'novel' pretends to mean new but names Samuel Richardson's eighteenth-century novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Richardson's epistolary work of 1748 bears this heroine's name as its title.

clue.text: There's f— all about the main obstacle: a rapid decline

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the outer phrase wraps round the obstacle

blocks.note: the phrase split open as F...ALL
a reef is a hazard in the main, the open sea

explanation.surface: A complaint that there is nothing at all standing in the way, leading to a sharp slump.
explanation.walkthrough: The censored 'f— all' supplies F and ALL with the reef between them; 'the main' is a poetic name for the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Free fall describes an uncontrolled plunge, as in prices or fortunes dropping fast.

clue.text: Dildo, capless, wet, bedraggled when boat hits bottom?

indicators.note: without its cap, the word loses its top, which in a down clue is its first letter
something bedraggled is messed up and dishevelled, so these letters are put in disorder

blocks.note: the word minus its first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smutty image of a soggy, dishevelled sex toy, with a nautical double entendre at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: At the ebb, when the sea is lowest, a moored boat may sit on the seabed.

clue.text: Show one's behind constitutional steps, as Michael Jackson would do

definitions.text: steps, as Michael Jackson would do

blocks.note: to moon is to bare one's backside
a constitutional is a walk taken for one's health

explanation.surface: Someone exposing their bottom while out for a healthy stroll.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Jackson's signature dance move gliding backwards is this, a sequence of steps.

clue.text: Got hurt protecting balls in Santa's place?

indicators.note: a hurt thing is damaged, so the letters are knocked out of order
to protect is to shield by surrounding, so the outer letters enclose the rest

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
balls and rot both mean nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone got injured in the groin, perhaps at a Christmas visit to Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks anatomical but means nonsense; the rearranged word splits after its first letter to take it in.
explanation.definitionFit: Department stores set up a Christmas grotto where children visit Father Christmas.

clue.text: (& 19dn.) MPs as a whole honest? Unlikely when protecting company millions

indicators.note: an unlikely version of the word is an improbable one, so its letters are rearranged
to protect is to surround and shield, so the rearranged letters go round the rest

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
CO is the abbreviation for company
M stands for million, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A cynical jibe that MPs are hardly honest when shielding firms worth millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honest? Unlikely' reads as a sneer at MPs, but 'Unlikely' is only the anagram signal acting on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The House of Commons is the elected chamber, the body of MPs taken collectively.

clue.text: (+ 22dn.) Lackey's boxers possibly getting stiff

blocks.note: boxers are a breed of dog
a stiff is slang for a corpse

explanation.surface: A servant's underpants getting aroused.
explanation.walkthrough: Boxers look like shorts and stiff like an adjective; they are a dog breed and a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogsbody is a menial drudge who does everyone else's chores, much like a lackey.

clue.text: A faction of Labour is enjoying having relinquished seats?

indicators.note: a faction is a part of a larger group, so a run of letters is taken from the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the next two

explanation.surface: Part of the Labour Party seems pleased to have given up its parliamentary seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seats' suggests parliament, but people who have stood up have literally relinquished their seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has risen has got up from a chair, so they have given up their seat.

clue.text: Short jumpers on the First Lady (large) start to titillate the president

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: roo is a short form of kangaroo, an animal that jumps
Eve was the first woman in Genesis
L is the abbreviation for large
first letter of titillate

explanation.surface: A saucy picture of a large First Lady in skimpy sweaters exciting the president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpers' looks like British sweaters, and 'First Lady' a president's wife; they are kangaroos and Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Two US presidents, Theodore and Franklin D., bore this surname.

clue.text: (& 17dn.) Archer and Aitken, once? Counsel's tip is to reform (they were hardly Thatcher's style)

definitions.note: the definition is phrased as a plural, the answer is singular

indicators.note: to reform is to form again in a new shape, so these letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: Jeffrey Archer and Jonathan Aitken, Tory politicians, both served prison sentences
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Two disgraced Tory ex-ministers, and a lawyer's advice that the system be reformed, contrasted with Thatcher's approach.
explanation.walkthrough: Archer (perjury) and Aitken (perjury) were jailed, so they are ex-convicts. Margaret Thatcher famously scorned seeking agreement across parties.
explanation.definitionFit: Thatcher called consensus 'the absence of leadership', so policy built by broad agreement was never her approach.

clue.text: see 25dn.
Very expensive picture of Lily, say, in tabloid (Sunday)

indicators.note: in places the plant name inside the newspaper name and its Sunday abbreviation

blocks.note: the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a lily is an example of a flower
S is the abbreviation for Sunday

explanation.surface: A costly photograph of a woman called Lily printed in the Sunday tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: Lily looks like a woman's name, perhaps Lily Allen in the Sun, but it is the plant. Van Gogh's Sunflowers sold for a record price in 1987.
explanation.definitionFit: Van Gogh's paintings of sunflowers sell for tens of millions, making them famously costly pictures.

clue.text: Reversed a line on shit hot game of ringing for a prize

definitions.text: game of ringing for a prize

indicators.note: reversed means turned round, so the whole string is read from its end back to its start

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line
poo is a childish word for excrement
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A crude account of someone reversing a line of cocaine onto something unpleasant at a fairground game.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoopla is the fairground game where players throw rings over prizes to win them.

clue.text: see 13ac.
It keeps a member rigid and new during break

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so one letter is placed inside the other word

blocks.note: to split is to break
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A smutty innuendo about something keeping an organ stiff, set during a holiday break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests the obvious innuendo, but it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: A splint is a rigid strip bound to a broken limb to hold it still while it heals.

clue.text: Solemnly promising to shove organ into rock

indicators.note: shoving one thing into another pushes it inside, putting it within the second word

blocks.note: to rock is to swing to and fro
the ear is an organ of the body

explanation.surface: A vow to push an organ into a rock, with a hint of something ruder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like a noun (a stone or music) but is a verb meaning to sway.
explanation.definitionFit: Swearing an oath means formally pledging, so it is a synonym of solemnly promising.

clue.text: see 9dn.
Take Tebbit's famous advice to embrace working? Twister!

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: Norman Tebbit said his father 'got on his bike' to look for work
on means working, as a switched-on machine

explanation.surface: Following Norman Tebbit's advice to get on your bike and find a job turns out to be a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman Tebbit, a Thatcher-era Conservative minister, told the unemployed in 1981 that his father 'got on his bike and looked for work'.
explanation.definitionFit: Twister is an informal name for a tornado, a violent rotating storm akin to the answer.

clue.text: In bad taste, Clinton's vice – just what the circling vultures want?

definitions.text: just what the circling vultures want?

blocks.note: food that tastes bad has gone off
Al Gore was Bill Clinton's vice president

explanation.surface: A dig at Bill Clinton's notorious vice, with scandal-hungry vultures overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' invites thoughts of Clinton's sexual scandals; it means his vice-president, Al Gore.
explanation.definitionFit: Offal is the entrails and organs of a carcass, the scraps scavenging birds feed on.

clue.text: As a corporation, pisspoor Beeb really lacks one

indicators.note: lacking one means going without a single item, here the letter that stands for one
something piss-poor is shoddily made, so these letters are put into a botched order

blocks.note: taken as written; the Beeb is a nickname for the BBC
the word without A, which stands for one

explanation.surface: A jibe that the BBC, a public corporation, is shamefully lacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' looks like the BBC's legal status; it is an old jocular word for a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is dated British slang for a large paunch, exactly what drinking ale builds.

clue.text: see 10dn.
Through securing the thingy with chain, which is nasty

indicators.note: securing means holding fast, so the outer word grips the others inside it

blocks.note: by means through, as in 'by way of'
it stands for an unnamed thing
CH is the abbreviation for chain, a unit of length

explanation.surface: A kinky image of something nasty secured with a chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitchy means spiteful or malicious in remarks, a synonym for nasty.

clue.text: Tory, a mud-splattered right old queen

indicators.note: something splattered is spread messily about, so these letters scatter into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician, smeared with scandal, described as a proper old queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old queen' plays on the slang for an older gay man; it means a historical monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary I, a Tudor, was Queen of England from 1553 to 1558, a monarch of long ago.

clue.text: (& 14ac.) Bum on bum, dead tight

blocks.note: a bum and a rat are both a worthless, contemptible person
bum and arse both mean backside
D is the abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: Rump on rump, packed really close together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' looks like snug, but is slang for drunk; the first bum is a lowlife, the second a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat-arsed is British slang for extremely drunk, and tight is an older slang synonym for inebriated.

clue.text: In toto, we lose, as the Aussies thrash us?

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following words, held within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A rueful English cricket fan conceding total defeat as Australia trounce them.
explanation.walkthrough: Throwing in the towel suggests surrender, but here the word is Australian slang meaning to beat someone up.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang, to towel someone (or towel them up) is to give them a beating.

clue.text: Bill possibly once holding back sex

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible arrangement of the letters, not the given one
back means going backwards, so the word is read from end to start
holding means gripping inside, so the outer letters enclose the others

blocks.note: the word rearranged
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A man named Bill who once held back from sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is a poster.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill is a printed poster or announcement, and a notice is a sign displaying information.

clue.text: Rt Hon. involved with EU corruption and casually at large

indicators.note: corruption is a debased, altered state, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the abbreviated title of a Privy Counsellor
taken as written
'n' is a casual form of and, as in rock 'n' roll

explanation.surface: A senior politician mixed up in European Union corruption, and now fled from justice.
explanation.walkthrough: Rt Hon. is the title of a British Privy Counsellor, given to cabinet ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugitive at large has escaped capture, which is the same as fleeing the law.
